task_statement:
Research question (as posed on 2026-10-06, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
A defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 120 team-seasons

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

research_concepts: regression to the mean and score effects
methodological_questions: Is a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change stable across split halves or seasons?
How much of H2-H1 change is regression to the mean, game state or garbage time?
Is 120 team-seasons enough to detect a reliable team-level trait?
Does a permutation or placebo test separate a defense effect from noise?

historical_evidence.finding: Split-half reliability of connector quality Q_p (n=102) was low: Pearson r=+0.215, Spearman-Brown ~0.355, ICC 0.216 (78.4% within-player variance). [prior work] states this is too low to treat Q_p as a stable scoutable trait. Limited by low measurement reliability.

Defensive scheme change within and across games (inferred labels) showed change in 99% of units, with near-uniform transition matrices. [prior work] states the inferred label cannot separate real defensive adjustment from the offense executing differently, and the pattern is consistent with label noise. Limited by label error.
The oracle best player for a counter play type varies by opponent (64/78 cells have more than one oracle player). This concerns matchup specificity, not H2-H1 change or team-trait reliability.

Play-type PPP change across playoff series game buckets showed no clear signal. [prior work] lists selection or regression to the mean as a limit, notes no CIs, and describes the data as observational.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Treating a half-split on-off PPP gap as a stable attribute
failed_approaches.why: Low measurement reliability: most variance is within-unit between halves (recorded as [prior work]).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Inferring defensive adjustment from labeled scheme changes
failed_approaches.why: Label or classification error; the label cannot distinguish defensive adjustment from offensive execution (recorded as [prior work]).

failed_approaches.what_failed: Reading change across game buckets as a systematic effect
failed_approaches.why: Selection or regression to the mean; [prior work] gives no clear signal (recorded as [prior work]).

evidence_establishes: Earlier project work found that a split-half difference-type metric at the player level had low reliability ([prior work][prior work], recorded untestable).
Earlier project work found that inferred defensive adjustment labels were too noisy to identify adjustment ([prior work][prior work], recorded untestable).
Earlier project work found that change-across-time comparisons in playoff data were exposed to selection and regression to the mean ([prior work][prior work], recorded inconclusive).
evidence_does_not_establish: No retrieved record directly measures the reliability of a team's defensive effect on opponents' H2-H1 change.
[prior work] do not show whether such a trait exists at the team level over full regular seasons.
[prior work] do not give a team-level noise variance for H2-H1 differences or a power calculation for 120 team-seasons.
[prior work][prior work] is not informative about the question.
own_inferences: An H2-H1 difference of opponent scoring is a difference score. Its between-team variance is likely small relative to game-level noise, so reliability is likely low, similar to the low reliability recorded in [prior work][prior work]. This is an analogy, not a finding.

Opponent H2-H1 change is confounded with the defense's own offense, lead and garbage time, rest and fatigue, and the quality of the opposing team. These effects could produce stable team differences that are not a defense trait.
Reliability should be estimated at the team-season level with odd/even-game splits and across adjacent seasons, using opponent-adjusted, score-state-controlled H2-H1 residuals.
Because the question asks about a trait, the claim is mainly about between-team variance. A variance-components estimate (ICC) with a permutation null is the right quantity, not a mean effect.
uncertainties: The unit of analysis (team-season or team-game), and whether the 120 team-seasons include playoffs, is unclear. Playoff team-seasons are few and have small samples.
The definition of 'effect on opponents' H2-H1 change' is not specified: points per possession, eFG, or points per 100, and how it is adjusted for the opponent's own H1 level.
Roster turnover between seasons will limit cross-season stability even if a within-season trait exists.
The 2025-26 season data may be partial or complete depending on the date, and this affects the data version.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved records do not answer the question, but they show repeated failures from low split-half reliability, noisy labels and regression to the mean in related questions. This moved the decision from a plain proceed to proceed_with_changes with a reliability-first design and a pre-specified stop rule.

blocking_constraints.text: The H2-H1 difference score is noisy, and reliability may be too low to show a trait.
With 120 team-seasons, only moderate reliabilities (about 0.25 or higher) can be detected, and cross-season tests use fewer pairs.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved record tests team-level reliability of defense-induced H2-H1 change. Related records show low reliability, label noise and regression to the mean in nearby questions.

risks.text: Difference scores have low reliability, and a defense effect may be dominated by within-team noise.
Teams selected on extreme H2-H1 change in one half or season will regress. Evaluate on all teams, not extremes.
Opponent quality, the defense's own offense, score state and garbage time, rest, pace and bench usage all affect H2-H1 change.
There are only 120 team-seasons, and playoff team-seasons have few games.
A trait claim needs a permutation null (shuffled opponent assignment) to show that between-team variance exceeds chance.
Opponent H2-H1 change is negatively correlated with H1 level (a mechanical regression component), so it must be adjusted for the opponent's H1 level.
Rule, roster and league-wide scoring changes across seasons may shift H2-H1 baselines.
Several metrics, splits and subsets would inflate false positives unless fixed in advance.

design.estimand: Between-team variance share (ICC / split-half reliability) of the opponent H2-H1 change in points per 100 possessions, adjusted for opponent H1 level, opponent quality, and score state. The question is whether the defensive team-season component is stable, and the secondary estimand is its year-to-year correlation for the same franchise.
design.unit: Team-season (defense), regular season only for the primary test, built from game-level opponent H2-H1 residuals. Playoffs are exploratory.
design.sample: Regular seasons 2022-23 through 2025-26 (complete since 2026-04-13). The primary analysis uses the 120 team-seasons. Exclude possessions in garbage time (pre-defined lead threshold in H2 clock), overtime, and games with missing halves. Freeze the data version at one date.
design.power: Compute from the noise variance observed in the data, before looking at the reliability. With about 80 games per team-season, odd/even split-half reliability of 0.25 or higher can be detected at roughly 80% power with n=120. Report the minimum detectable reliability. If the Spearman-Brown reliability CI upper bound is below 0.3, conclude the trait is not reliable enough to use.
design.controls: Model opponent H2-H1 change as a mixed model with opponent offense strength (season-level), opponent H1 PPP, home/away, rest days, pace, and H1 margin, with random effects for defense team-season and opponent team-season. Split games by odd/even index and by first/second half of the season. Also test year-to-year stability with roster continuity as a moderator.
design.falsification: Permutation null: shuffle defense labels within opponent and season (at least 5,000 permutations) to obtain the null distribution of ICC. Placebo: apply the same procedure to an outcome that should show no defense trait, such as H1-only first-quarter versus second-quarter change. Negative control: compare against reliability of the defenses' H2-H1 change in their own offensive performance.
design.multiplicity: One primary metric (points per 100 possessions) and one primary test (split-half ICC with the permutation null). Secondary metrics (eFG, turnover rate, free throw rate) are exploratory with Holm correction over the secondary family.
design.decision_rule: Supported if the adjusted split-half reliability is at least 0.30 with the lower 95% CI bound above 0 and the permutation p < 0.05, and the cross-season correlation is positive with CI excluding 0. Rejected if the upper CI bound of reliability is below 0.20. Otherwise report as inconclusive. Do not choose cut-offs after seeing results.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game play-by-play and box-score files for the 2022-23 to 2025-26 regular seasons, frozen with a recorded date; playoff 2025-26 data complete from 2026-06-21 may be added only as an exploratory set.
